title: Burying his mother in Savannah and the policeman at the wake
summary: At his mother's wake white musician friends came, and a polite policeman asked them to leave.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You know, I remember I went home to bury my mother in about -- around 1940, and Savannah, Georgia is a funny place. In '40 they weren't too open with things down there. But some of the -- my friends, the Caucasian friends I had down there knew I was coming and my mother had died -- musicians. Man, they had a flock of them around my house, you know, a whole bunch of them was around my house when I got there.

So, you know, down South when somebody's dead, you have a wake. You know, three or four days of drinking and food and everything there. So, there was a lot of liquor and everything in the house. And we were drinking. We were sitting on

the front porch, talking and shooting the breeze, smoking. And a policeman came by there and he called me. He says -- very nicely he says, he said, I know your mother just passed and I know you live in New York now. He says, I just thought I'd -- he says, we had a call, you know, that were a lot of mixing over here and everything like that. He says, and I know it's a solemn occasion. I had to come by to tell you this but, you know, some of the people in your neighborhood are afraid that something bad might happen because (unintelligible) bad might happen, you know, behind it.

So, he says, you know, I just advise you, you know, to let the -- I'm sorry. I don't like to bring this kind of message, but let the fellows -- tell the fellows they have to go home. So, I told them and, you know, I thanked him because he was real straight the way he came on with it. And the guys were really -- they were really drugged by the whole scene. But they had to go, you know.
But they could have sent a nasty one over there too, by the same token. You know, so they wasn't ready yet, you know. This was the '40's so, you know, I imagine it's a lot better now.
